lesson.title: From One Sample to the Whole Population: The Big Idea of Inference
lesson.summary: Statistical inference is the general process of using a sample statistic and its known sampling distribution to draw reasoned conclusions about an unknown population parameter.
lesson.body:
Every real world statistics problem starts with the same frustrating fact: you almost never get to measure the entire population. You have a parameter you care about, some true, fixed but unknown number describing the whole population, such as the true proportion of voters who support a policy or the true average commute time in a city. What you actually have is a statistic, a number computed from a sample, such as a sample proportion or a sample mean. Statistical inference is the formal set of methods for bridging that gap: using a statistic, plus what we know about how much that statistic varies from sample to sample, to make a reasoned, quantified statement about the parameter.

The reason this is even possible traces back to the sampling distribution. If a sample statistic wandered around unpredictably with no describable pattern, there would be no honest way to reason from a single sample back to the population. But the sampling distribution tells us the statistic's average behavior and its typical spread across repeated samples. That structure is what lets inference work: instead of treating a sample statistic as a lucky or unlucky guess, we can describe exactly how much uncertainty surrounds it and build that uncertainty into our conclusions.

Statistical inference generally takes two forms, both of which rest on this same foundation. Estimation uses a sample statistic to pin down a plausible value, or range of values, for the unknown parameter. Hypothesis testing, a topic for later chapters, uses a sample statistic to evaluate whether a specific claim about the parameter is believable. This unit focuses entirely on the estimation branch, building up to confidence intervals, which are the standard tool for expressing our best guess for the parameter along with how much uncertainty surrounds that guess.

Suppose a researcher wants to estimate p, the true proportion of all adults in a large city who support a proposed transit measure. A random sample of 400 adults is surveyed, and 100 of them support the measure. The sample statistic is p-hat equals 100 divided by 400, which equals 0.25. That single number, 0.25, is a reasonable guess at the unknown parameter p, but statistical inference asks for more than a guess. Using the formula for the standard deviation of a sample proportion, the sampling distribution of p-hat here has a standard deviation of the square root of (0.25 times 0.75) divided by 400, which works out to about 0.0217. That number quantifies how much p-hat would typically bounce around from sample to sample of this size, and it is the raw material the next several chapters use to turn the single number 0.25 into a full statement of estimated precision, first as a point estimate, and then as an interval estimate.
